items.text: What is a merger (integration) clause, and what did UAW-GM Human Resource Center v KSL Recreation Corp hold about its effect?

A merger clause states the written contract is the entire agreement. UAW-GM v KSL, 228 Mich App 486 (1998), held that a valid integration clause is conclusive proof the contract is fully integrated, and it nullifies all antecedent (earlier) agreements.
Under UAW-GM v KSL, once a contract has a valid merger clause, when can outside evidence of an earlier verbal promise still be used to change the deal?

Only in cases of fraud that invalidate the integration clause itself, or fraud that invalidates the entire contract including the merger clause. A bare claim that the other side said something different verbally is not enough.
TRAP: Does a general claim of fraud during contract negotiations defeat a valid merger clause in Michigan?

No. UAW-GM v KSL holds the only fraud that can vitiate the contract is fraud relating to the merger clause itself, or fraud invalidating the entire contract including the merger clause. Ordinary negotiation fraud about some other fact is not enough on its own.

A subcontractor signs a one-page work order with a merger clause. The GC's superintendent verbally promised extra pay for mold work during the walk-through, but the signed work order says nothing about it. Mold turns up. Can the sub enforce the verbal promise?

Almost certainly not. Under UAW-GM v KSL, the merger clause nullifies the earlier verbal promise unless the sub can show fraud relating to the merger clause itself or fraud invalidating the whole contract. The lesson is to get any promise that matters written into the signed document before signing.
What court decided UAW-GM Human Resource Center v KSL Recreation Corp, and when?
The Michigan Court of Appeals, March 6, 1998, published.
Normally, before deciding whether a contract is fully integrated, what can a court look at? What does a valid merger clause change about that?

Normally a court can look at parol evidence (outside evidence of prior or contemporaneous talks) to decide the threshold integration question. UAW-GM v KSL holds that a valid merger clause is conclusive on integration by itself, skipping that evidentiary step.
In a contract, what is the difference between a duty to indemnify and a duty to defend?

Indemnify means to pay for an established loss, in dollars, after the loss is determined. Defend means to fund or provide the defense, usually legal defense costs, while a claim is pending, before anyone knows who ultimately owes what. They can be owed on different timelines.
What is "hold harmless," and how is it generally treated relative to "indemnify"?

Hold harmless is commonly treated by courts and commentators as functionally the same as indemnify: a promise not to pursue the other party for the loss. This is general commentary, not independently tied to a Michigan holding.
What did American Bumper & Mfg Co v Hartford Fire Ins Co hold about the relative scope of the duty to defend and the duty to indemnify?

"[T]he scope of the two duties is not identical; the duty to defend is broader than the duty to indemnify." American Bumper & Mfg Co v Hartford Fire Ins Co, 452 Mich 440 (1996), Michigan Supreme Court.
In Auto-Owners Ins Co v City of Clare, what standard triggers the duty to defend?

The duty to defend is triggered when coverage is "even arguably within the coverage," and arises "in instances in which coverage is even arguable, though the claim may be groundless or frivolous." Auto-Owners Ins Co v City of Clare, 446 Mich 1 (1994).
TRAP: Are American Bumper and Auto-Owners v City of Clare general commercial-contract indemnity cases, or something narrower?

Narrower. Both are insurance-duty cases describing an insurer's duty to defend its own policyholder. No Michigan case applying the identical "defend is broader than indemnify" rule to a non-insurance commercial indemnification clause (such as a GC-subcontractor agreement) was opened this run; that extension is practitioner logic, not a cited Michigan holding.

A mitigation subcontract requires the sub to "indemnify, defend, and hold harmless" the GC for claims arising from the sub's work. A homeowner sues the GC over a slip-and-fall on wet flooring the sub left uncovered, before anyone has determined fault. Can the defend obligation matter immediately?

Yes. The defend obligation can require the sub to fund or provide the GC's legal defense as the lawsuit proceeds, independent of whether the sub is ultimately found liable. The separate indemnify question, who actually pays if there is a judgment or settlement, is decided later. Treating "indemnify, defend, and hold harmless" as one single obligation misses that the defend duty can bite immediately, win or lose.
What does MCL 440.2719(1)(b) say about an agreed contract remedy, unless the parties make it exclusive?
"[R]esort to a remedy as provided is optional unless the remedy is expressly agreed to be exclusive, in which case it is the sole remedy." MCL 440.2719(1)(b).
Under MCL 440.2719(2), what happens if an exclusive or limited contract remedy fails of its essential purpose?

"Where circumstances cause an exclusive or limited remedy to fail of its essential purpose, remedy may be had as provided in this act." In plain words, if the one remedy the contract gives turns out worthless in practice, the law reopens ordinary remedies.
Under MCL 440.2719(3), when can consequential damages be limited or excluded, and what is different about a consumer-goods personal-injury limitation?

Consequential damages may be limited or excluded unless the limitation is unconscionable. A limitation of consequential damages for personal injury in the case of consumer goods is "prima facie unconscionable," but a limitation where the loss is commercial is not.
What did Xu v Gay hold about using a contractual waiver of liability to insulate against gross negligence?
"A contractual waiver of liability also serves to insulate against ordinary negligence, but not gross negligence." Xu v Gay, 257 Mich App 263 (2003), Michigan Court of Appeals.
How did Xu v Gay define gross negligence?
"Conduct so reckless as to demonstrate a substantial lack of concern for whether an injury results." Xu v Gay, 257 Mich App 263 (2003).
Why do well-drafted limitation-of-liability clauses usually carve out gross negligence, willful misconduct, fraud, and breach of indemnification obligations?

Because a court may refuse to enforce a liability cap against those categories anyway. Xu v Gay bars contracting out of liability for gross negligence; drafters write the carve-out explicitly so the rest of the cap still holds for ordinary negligence.
A rented dehumidifier's thermostat fails through ordinary equipment wear and starts a fire. The rental agreement caps the company's liability at the rental fee paid. Does the cap likely hold?
Likely yes. An ordinary equipment failure is the kind of loss a limitation-of-liability clause is meant to cap, and nothing here rises to gross negligence or willful misconduct under Xu v Gay's line.

Same rental agreement and cap, but this time the technician deliberately disabled a known safety shutoff to make the unit "work better," and that choice caused the fire. Does the cap still protect the rental company?

Probably not. Deliberately disabling a known safety feature looks like conduct a court could call grossly negligent or willful, and Xu v Gay, 257 Mich App 263 (2003), holds a contractual waiver cannot insulate against gross negligence.
How did Harbor Park Market, Inc v Gronda define a "condition precedent"?

"A fact or event that the parties intend must take place before there is a right to performance." Harbor Park Market, Inc v Gronda, 277 Mich App 126 (2007), quoting Mikonczyk v Detroit Newspapers, Inc.
What is the practical difference between a covenant and a condition precedent if the triggering requirement is never satisfied?

A covenant is a plain promise; breaking it is a breach, and the other side can sue for damages. A condition precedent is a fact or event that must happen before any right to performance exists; if it never happens, there may be no breach claim at all, because the obligation never came into existence.
What words in a contract typically signal a condition rather than a plain promise?
Words like "subject to," "provided that," "on condition that," and "if and only if" typically signal a condition. A plain "shall" or "will" typically signals a covenant.
In Harbor Park Market v Gronda, what was the actual clause at issue, and how did the court read it?

The purchase agreement stated it was "subject to review & approval of attorney [named] on or before [date]." Both the trial court and the parties treated that attorney-approval clause as a condition precedent, and the Court of Appeals agreed the clause's language compelled that reading.
TRAP: Does Harbor Park Market v Gronda establish a blanket rule that "subject to" always creates a condition precedent in every Michigan contract?

No. The court cautioned that Michigan courts are "not inclined to construe stipulations of a contract as conditions precedent" unless the contract's clear language compels it. Harbor Park Market's holding rests on this specific clause's wording, not a free-standing drafting canon applied across all contracts.

A mitigation contract says payment is due "subject to the insurance carrier's approval of the estimate," and the carrier never approves it. Under Harbor Park Market's framework, does the contractor have a breach-of-contract claim against the homeowner for nonpayment?

Likely not, if that language is read as a condition precedent: the triggering event, carrier approval, never happened, so the homeowner's payment obligation never came into existence. A contractor who wants to be paid regardless of carrier approval needs a plain covenant instead, such as "Homeowner shall pay within 30 days of completion."
What is Michigan's default rule on whether time is "of the essence" in a contract, per MacRitchie v Plumb?

"Time is not to be regarded as of the essence of a contract unless made so by express provision of the parties." Time can also become essential "by the nature of the contract itself" or by "the circumstances under which the contract was executed." MacRitchie v Plumb, 70 Mich App 242 (1976).
Without a "time is of the essence" clause, is missing a completion date usually a material breach in Michigan?

No, usually not. Missing a date is ordinarily a minor breach (the other side can seek delay damages, but the contract stays in force) unless the contract expressly makes time essential, or the nature of the deal or circumstances of signing show it was.
What does adding a "time is of the essence" clause change about the legal effect of a missed deadline?

It flips the default: a missed deadline, even a short one, can be treated as a material breach, meaning the other side can walk away from the whole contract and sue, rather than just collecting delay damages while staying bound.

A reconstruction contract says, "time is of the essence; Contractor shall complete all work by August 15." The contractor finishes five days late because of a supply delay outside anyone's control. What is the homeowner's strongest argument, and why does the clause matter here?

The homeowner can argue the five-day miss is itself a material breach, not just a minor delay, because the time-is-of-the-essence clause flips Michigan's default rule from MacRitchie v Plumb. Without that clause, the same five-day slip would ordinarily be a minor breach only.
What court decided MacRitchie v Plumb, and when?
The Michigan Court of Appeals, July 20, 1976.
What is the "American Rule" on attorney fees, as stated in Great Lakes Shores, Inc v Bartley?
"Attorney fees are not recoverable from a losing party unless authorized by a statute, court rule, or other recognized exception." Great Lakes Shores, Inc v Bartley, 311 Mich App 252 (2015).
Under Great Lakes Shores v Bartley, is a contractual fee-shifting clause a recognized exception to the American Rule?
Yes. "One such other exception is when attorney fees are recoverable pursuant to a contract between the parties," and "such contractual provisions are enforceable."
What is the difference between a mutual ("prevailing party") fee-shifting clause and a one-way fee-shifting clause?

A mutual clause lets whichever side wins collect fees from the loser, changing both sides' incentive to settle rather than fight a marginal claim. A one-way clause lets only one named party collect fees if it wins, and exposes the other side to that risk regardless of who actually wins.

A referral-network vendor agreement says, "Contractor shall pay Company's reasonable attorney fees incurred in any dispute arising from this Agreement," with no mention of the Company paying the contractor's fees if the contractor wins. Is this a mutual or a one-way fee-shifting clause, and what does that mean for the contractor?

One-way. It only ever exposes the contractor to the Company's legal bill in a dispute; the contractor gets no reciprocal right to collect fees even if the contractor wins. Read every fee clause for this kind of asymmetry before signing, because it changes who can afford to fight a disputed claim.
What court decided Great Lakes Shores, Inc v Bartley, and when was it approved for publication?
The Michigan Court of Appeals; approved for publication July 2, 2015.
What does MCL 600.745(3) require a Michigan court to do when the parties agreed in writing to litigate only in another state, and the action is filed in Michigan anyway?
The court "shall dismiss or stay the action, as appropriate," unless one of five listed exceptions applies.
List the five exceptions in MCL 600.745(3) that let a Michigan court keep a case despite an out-of-state forum-selection clause.

(a) a statute requires the Michigan court to hear it; (b) the plaintiff cannot get effective relief in the other state for reasons other than delay; (c) the other state is substantially less convenient than Michigan; (d) the agreement was obtained by misrepresentation, duress, abuse of economic power, or other unconscionable means; (e) it would for some other reason be unfair or unreasonable to enforce the agreement.
What did Turcheck v Amerifund Financial, Inc say about Michigan's general policy on enforcing forum-selection clauses?

"Michigan courts generally enforce contractual forum-selection clauses," citing MCL 600.745(3); "unless one of the statutory exceptions applies, Michigan courts will enforce a forum-selection clause as written"; and "Michigan's public policy favors the enforcement of contractual forum-selection clauses." Turcheck v Amerifund Financial, Inc, 272 Mich App 341 (2006).
What is the difference between a forum-selection clause and a venue clause?

A forum-selection clause picks the court system (and often the state) where a dispute must be litigated. A venue clause (sometimes the same clause) picks the specific county or district within that system.
TRAP: Is the jury-trial-waiver case commonly cited in Michigan practice, Andy J Egan Co v Pro Services, Inc (2018), independently verified in this corpus?

No. The opinion could not be located and opened at a confirmed URL this run. Do not quote or cite its specific holding without opening the actual opinion first; its content is flagged [INSUFFICIENT_DATA] in this domain.

A large commercial-property owner's standard work-order form requires any dispute to be filed only in a specific out-of-state county, with a jury-trial waiver in the same paragraph. A restoration company signs it without reading closely. What has the company agreed to in advance?

It has agreed, in advance, to travel out of state and argue the case to a judge alone if a change-order dispute ever goes to litigation. Under Turcheck and MCL 600.745(3), Michigan courts generally enforce that kind of forum-selection clause as written absent one of the statute's five exceptions, which is exactly why the combination can make a modest dispute too expensive to pursue at all.
In ordinary contract drafting, is the word "including" exhaustive (a closed list) or non-exhaustive (examples only) by default?

Non-exhaustive by default. "Covered losses include fire, wind, and theft" ordinarily means those are examples of a broader category, not the only three things covered, unless the contract pins the word down with language like "including, and limited to" or "including only." This is a general drafting and interpretation canon, not a Michigan-specific statutory rule or holding verified this run.
How does a careful drafter write a genuinely closed list, if a bare "including" is read as non-exhaustive?
By writing "means" instead of "includes," or by writing "including, and limited to," instead of a bare "including."

A subcontract scope-of-work section says the sub's price "includes labor, materials, and equipment rental." A dispute arises over whether permit fees are part of that price, since permit fees are not listed. Does the non-exhaustive reading of "includes" automatically help the sub or the GC?

Neither side automatically. Because "includes" is read as illustrative, not a closed list, permit fees could still be read as included even though unlisted, which can cut against the sub just as easily as it can cut in the sub's favor on a different missing item. The fix is drafting a genuinely closed list up front, not arguing the canon after a dispute starts.
What did Manuel v Gill hold about the words "may" and "shall"?
The term "may" is "permissive," as opposed to the term "shall," which is considered "mandatory." Manuel v Gill, 481 Mich 637 (2008), Michigan Supreme Court, decided July 16, 2008.
TRAP: Does Manuel v Gill establish the shall/may default as a rule of private-contract interpretation?

Not directly. Manuel v Gill construes a statute, not a private contract. The shall/may default it states is also standard general contract-drafting usage, but citing Manuel v Gill as if it were a contract-interpretation holding overstates it; flag that usage as [SECONDARY] when applied to a private contract.
What does "will" signal in careful contract drafting, as opposed to "shall"?

"Will" is grammatically a statement about the future (background fact), not an obligation. Careful drafters avoid using "will" to create a duty, reserving "shall" for mandatory obligations and "may" for permissive options. No Michigan contract case specifically addressing "will" as a drafting signal was opened this run; this point is general drafting commentary, flagged [INSUFFICIENT_DATA] as Michigan contract-case authority.

A work-authorization form says, "Homeowner may cancel this agreement within three business days," and elsewhere, "Contractor shall begin mitigation work within 24 hours of authorization." Under the shall/may default, which obligation is mandatory and which is optional?
The contractor's 24-hour start is mandatory ("shall"). The homeowner's cancellation right is permissive ("may"): it is hers to use or not, not a duty she must exercise.

The same work-authorization form later says, "Contractor will submit a final invoice within 10 days." A sloppy reading treats this the same as the "shall" clauses. What should a careful reader flag instead?

That "will" is the odd word out among a contract that otherwise uses "shall" for duties and "may" for options, and ask whether the drafter actually meant "shall." Mixing shall, may, and will in similar-looking clauses invites exactly the kind of ambiguity litigation a clean contract avoids.
What is the recommended order for reading any new contract, per this domain's method section?

First, find the merger clause. Second, find the clauses that move risk or money: indemnify/defend/hold-harmless and limitation of liability. Third, find the clauses that control whether you even have a claim: conditions precedent vs. covenants, and time-is-of-the-essence. Fourth, find the clauses controlling cost and location of a lawsuit: fee-shifting, venue, and jury waiver. Last, read the small words: "including" and shall/may/will.
This domain covers general contract law, not insurance policy law. How should a claim drawn only from general common law or the UCC, with no Michigan case or statute behind it, be labeled?

As general common-law or UCC doctrine, not Michigan-specific, and never dressed up as if a Michigan case decided it. Where no primary source was opened this run, the claim is labeled [INSUFFICIENT_DATA] and kept off cards.

A GC hands a subcontractor a dense five-page contract an hour before a job starts. Which three clause types from this domain should the sub scan for first, given how much leverage they can quietly shift?

The merger clause (does it erase any verbal promises made during the walk-through), the indemnify/defend/hold-harmless clause (who pays, and who funds defense, if a third party gets hurt), and the limitation-of-liability clause with its carve-outs (what is capped, and does the cap actually survive gross negligence or willful misconduct under Xu v Gay).
